newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss panel to review Holocaust clears key hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Swiss panel to review Holocaust clears key hurdle.

text.p: Switzerland's lower house of parliament voted on Monday for a sweeping study of Swiss financial dealings with Nazi Germany and the fate of Jewish wealth deposited before, during and after World War Two.
Acknowledging the strong international interest, the National Council endorsed a decree put forward by the cabinet and sent the measure for final approval to the upper chamber of parliament.

The 162-0 vote after two hours of discussion reflected support across the political spectrum and indicated final approval was likely for the panel that Swiss leaders hope will restore the country's international reputation.
"This is part of our history and, in the end, a question of our image and credibility," Lili Nabholz, president of the lower house's legal affairs commission, told her colleagues.
"What we are doing we are doing late, but it is never too late," she said.

The decree creates a commission of experts empowered to lift tight banking secrecy rules for a historical accounting of Swiss commerce with Nazi Germany, for whom Swiss gold purchases were a crucial source of funds to finance their war effort.

It will also review how much wealth was deposited with Swiss banks and other financial companies by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution and whether the Swiss have done enough to identify the lost assets of those killed in the Holocaust.

The move follows a recent burst of speculation, fuelled by newly declassified U.S. wartime archives, that Switzerland could still be hoarding Nazi gold or holding millions of dollars in assets from people who perished during Hitler's reign of terror.

Speakers at the debate agreed the review panel was needed amid unprecedented attacks from abroad, even though some noted Switzerland froze German assets after the war, turned them over to the Allies and has sought to track down Holocaust accounts.
But others were adamant that the Swiss finally had to face the past squarely and admit they were spared a Nazi invasion in part because they provided valuable services to wartime Germany.
"It is time to recognise our part of the guilt for the greatest catastrophe of the century," said Verena Grendelmeier, an independent who was a driving force pushing for the probe.

"The decree offers a unique chance for Switzerland to draw up a picture of itself that is close to reality," added Social Democrat Paul Rechsteiner, who said the country's current image of itself was based on "self-deception and lies".

Others were clearly miffed that Switzerland's record was being dragged through the mud by critics who paint the country as Hitler's willing collaborator rather than a small democracy worried about survival in the fascist Europe that surrounded it.
Some saw the latest attacks, primarily from Britain and the United States, as part of a conspiracy to dull Switzerland's competitive edge as an international financial centre.

"It is no coincidence that harsh tones are coming from the City of London and the New York senatorial campaign," said Marc Suter, a Liberal Democrat, referring to New York Senator Alfonse D'Amato's well-publicised interest in the case.
He said the onslaught may have been triggered in part "to weaken Switzerland as a financial centre and undermine banking secrecy".
Almost all speakers played down expectations, noting that many witnesses were dead and that banks had destroyed records of long-dormant accounts.

The commission, which could start work as early as April, is separate from an international panel set up by Swiss banks and world Jewish groups last May to search for any lost Holocaust accounts and help return the assets to their rightful owners.
